summary: Memorial lantern tower and time ball, dedicated April 15, 1913 on the Seamen's Church Institute roof; moved to Fulton and Pearl Streets in 1976; restored in 2026.

light.note: Fixed green light (LighthouseFriends, 1913 description). The museum's June 2026 post describes green lights glowing inside the lantern.

structures.name: Titanic Memorial Lighthouse
structures.type: lantern tower with time ball on a steel rod
structures.note: On the roof of the Seamen's Church Institute, 1913 to 1968. Top donated to the South Street Seaport Museum in July 1968; re-erected in May 1976 on a concrete podium at Fulton and Pearl Streets; restoration completed summer 2026 (museum). The record's 18.3 m agrees with the 60 ft figure on Wikipedia, which is not cited.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The museum's 2026 pages describe the time ball as visible to visitors in the park.

visit.note: Titanic Memorial Park at Fulton and Pearl Streets, at the entrance to the South Street Seaport Historic District.

events.note: Cornerstone of the new Seamen's Church Institute building laid one day after the sinking.
A week after the cornerstone, the institute announced the lighthouse atop the building would be a memorial to the victims.
Titanic Memorial Lighthouse and time ball dedicated April 15, 1913, a year after the sinking, on the roof of the Seamen's Church Institute at South Street and Coenties Slip.
Time ball put into operation November 1, 1913, activated by a telegraphic signal from the Naval Observatory.
Seamen's Church Institute put its building up for sale.
Daily noon drop of the time ball ended (LighthouseFriends gives 1913 to 1967). Rowlett's directory in the record also gives 1967.

Seamen's Church Institute moved to 15 State Street in July 1968. The building and lighthouse were set for demolition; the top of the tower was donated to the South Street Seaport Museum in July 1968 by Kaiser-Nelson Steel & Salvage Corporation.
Re-erected in May 1976 on a lighthouse-inspired concrete podium at the corner of Fulton and Pearl Streets, with funds from the Exxon Corporation.

Descendants of people connected with the Titanic called for restoration; Friends of the Titanic Lighthouse Restoration formed to refurbish and relight it (LighthouseFriends). Wikipedia dates plans to 2019; not used.
Museum selected preservation architects Jan Hird Pokorny Associates for the restoration.
Restoration of the artifact completed summer 2026; restored time ball raised and lowered daily around noon on a new rigging system.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1967 (Rowlett's). LighthouseFriends ends the daily time-ball drop in 1967, and the museum says the structure stayed at its original location until 1968. Both dates hold: 1967 is the end of the time ball's noon drop and 1968 is the move.
The record's coordinates (40.7074, -74.00386) match the 1976 site at Fulton and Pearl Streets. The USLHS position (41.1793, -74.0062) does not match any site in the sources read and is not used.

notes_for_editor: Sources read: LighthouseFriends (rich narrative, undated), two 1913 newspaper pages (the Evening World dedication report, OCR garbled in places, quoted as printed; the Tribune page is badly OCR'd, so only its headline words are quoted), and two museum pages from 2026. The NYT 1913 report that Wikipedia cites (about 200 persons present) was not read; the museum says nearly 300 attended, so crowd figures are left out of the story. Wikipedia (lead only, not cited): 60 ft (18 m) height, dedication 1913, restoration plans 2019, LPC and architects. The record's status 'inactive' and the museum's 2026 description of working green lights and a daily time ball are not reconciled: whether the lantern works as an aid to navigation, and whether it is on the Coast Guard List of Lights, was not checked; the record should be reviewed by a person. The record's 'deactivated 1967' is in resolved_conflicts. The Seamen's Church Institute building design: the museum's sentence 'Designed by Warren & Wetmore' sits between descriptions of the memorial and the institute, so it is not used. No keeper, attendant or operator of the time ball is named in the sources read; the keepers and storms chapters are omitted, not because no one ran the time ball, but because none is named. A National Register application was planned (LighthouseFriends 2020; titaniclighthouse.org press page), but no listing was confirmed; not checked against the NPS database. The 1922 Lighthouse Service Bulletin mentions a barge named Titanic B-19 lost in Mississippi Sound, a different vessel with no link to this station. The Commissioner and Lighthouse Board reports do not cover this structure (a private memorial light). Peter Stanford is named only as the museum's founding president, in the museum's own account of his 1968 letter. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the Stanford letter is quoted from the museum page, not paraphrased. The Evening World OCR reads only Bishop tlreer, so the name David H. Greer comes from the LighthouseFriends page, which quotes the dedication. The Tribune OCR is poor: the story quotes only the two lines that read clearly, MANY SURVIVORS ATTEND and Time Ball and Light To Be Ready Soon. A malformed corrections entry (prose in current and proposed) was removed and its substance is kept here: the record's status note says no usable position, but the record coordinates (40.7074, -74.00386) match the 1976 Fulton and Pearl Streets site, and no coordinates for the 1913 to 1968 roof site were found in the sources read. A person should review the status note. The statement that the plaque coordinates lie in the Atlantic is a geographic inference from the numbers, not a sourced claim.
